The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents Panel has identified six on-field refereeing errors during the latest round of matches, equalling the highest number of mistakes recorded in a single weekend. The errors involved contentious decisions in matches featuring Arsenal, Everton, Liverpool, Crystal Palace, Ipswich Town and Bournemouth, according to a report by BBC Sport on Wednesday. The panel, comprising five members, reviews controversial incidents each week and votes on whether referees and video assistant referees made the correct decisions. The last time the panel recorded six on-field errors in a single weekend was during the early part of the 2023/24 season. However, the figure does not include correct VAR interventions that overturned mistakes, including the red card shown to Brentford forward Igor Thiago. Two of the six incidents were classified as errors by both the on-field referee and VAR, while four were considered incorrect refereeing decisions that did not meet the threshold for VAR intervention. One of the controversial incidents involved Everton defender James Tarkowski, who appeared to pull the hair of Coventry City’s Caleb Yirenkyi inside the penalty area. No penalty was awarded during the match, but the panel unanimously ruled the decision incorrect, voting 5-0 that both the referee and VAR should have intervened. The panel said, “Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi’s hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened.” Another incident involved Arsenal forward Kai Havertz, who was pulled down inside the penalty area by Hull City’s Nobel Mendy. Although VAR official Michael Oliver asked referee Farai Hallam to review the incident at the pitchside monitor, no penalty was awarded after Havertz was deemed to have been offside. It said, “Although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence.” Four other decisions ruled incorrect The panel also identified four other incidents in which the original refereeing decisions were considered wrong, although VAR intervention was not recommended. One involved Everton’s Thierno Barry, whose 61st-minute goal against Coventry City was reviewed for a possible handball. The panel voted 2-3 that the on-field decision was incorrect but unanimously agreed that VAR should not have intervened because the available footage did not provide conclusive evidence. On Liverpool’s match against Crystal Palace, the panel ruled that the late penalty awarded against the Reds for a challenge by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio was incorrect. It voted unanimously that the on-field decision was wrong but maintained that the incident did not constitute a clear and obvious error requiring VAR intervention. The spot kick was awarded in the 72nd minute after Lewis Cook was adjudged to have fouled Abdoul Ouattara. The panel voted 4-1 that the decision was incorrect, arguing that Ouattara had moved across Cook, who had not made a challenge. Another incident involved Bournemouth midfielder Marcus Tavernier, who was not shown a second yellow card despite deliberately delaying the restart of play. The panel voted 3-2 that the referee’s decision was incorrect, although the incident was not eligible for VAR intervention. Despite the number of errors recorded, the panel upheld several high-profile decisions that attracted criticism during the weekend. Tottenham Hotspur had questioned the decision not to send off Leeds United defender Jayden Bogle following a challenge on Mathys Tel. However, the panel voted 3-2 that the decision not to issue a red card was correct. The majority believed Bogle was attempting to challenge for the ball and that his contact with Tel’s ankle did not involve the speed, force or intensity required to constitute serious foul play. Chelsea forward Cole Palmer’s appeal for a penalty following contact with Sunderland’s Luke O’Nien was also rejected. The panel voted 4-1 that the decision to award a free kick rather than a penalty was correct, noting that the contact occurred outside the penalty area. Similarly, the panel unanimously supported the penalty awarded to Sunderland after Chelsea defender Levi Colwill was adjudged to have tripped Brian Bobbey. It also unanimously upheld the decision not to penalise Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens for his contact with Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu’s 96th-minute equaliser. The findings have renewed discussions about the effectiveness of VAR and the high threshold required for officials to overturn on-field decisions. The Key Match Incidents Panel plays an important role in assessing refereeing standards in the Premier League, with its findings contributing to a merit table that accounts for 50 per cent of referees’ salary bonus payments. Although supporters have frequently criticised controversial refereeing decisions, the panel maintains that its assessments are based on the Laws of the Game and the Premier League’s expected standards of officiating. The report noted that the six on-field errors, alongside the separate correct VAR intervention involving Thiago’s red card, highlighted the number of contentious decisions during the latest round of fixtures. However, the distinction between an incorrect on-field decision and an error requiring VAR intervention continues to generate frustration among supporters.
